cse-2025-1-cs-43.approach: The figure gives each level's **total** time for an access served there (the miss penalties are already included). So the AMAT is simply the weighted average of the three total times, weighted by the probability that the access is served at each level.
cse-2025-1-cs-43.given:
| Level | Hit rate | Total time if served here |
|---|---|---|
| L1 | 95% | 10 ns |
| L2 | 85% | 20 ns (includes L1 miss penalty) |
| Main memory | 100% | 200 ns (includes L1 and L2 miss penalty) |

steps.title: Read the times as totals
steps.body: The words "including L1 cache miss penalty" and "including L1 and L2 cache miss penalty" mean that 20 ns is the **whole** time of an access that misses L1 and hits L2, and 200 ns is the **whole** time of an access that misses both caches. Nothing must be added to them.

steps.title: Probability of being served at each level

pitfalls: Treating 20 ns and 200 ns as the access time of that level alone and adding them on top: $10 + 0.05(20 + 0.15\times 200) = 12.5$ ns, which double-counts the L1/L2 lookups.
Using $0.15$ (instead of $0.05\times 0.15 = 0.0075$) as the probability of going to main memory — the L2 hit rate is a *local* rate among L1 misses.
Forgetting that every access pays at least the 10 ns L1 lookup when using the "extra time" form.
cse-2025-1-cs-43.verification: Two independent forms agree: the weighted average of total times ($9.5+0.85+1.5$) and the base-plus-extra form ($10+0.5+1.35$) both give $11.85$ ns, inside the key range 11.83–11.87.

cse-2025-1-cs-44.approach: Simulate reference by reference. On a fault with all frames full, look only at the window of the next 4 references (current one included) and evict the resident page whose next use in that window is farthest away — a page that does not appear in the window at all goes first.
cse-2025-1-cs-44.given: Reference string: $1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4$ (12 references), 3 frames, initially empty; on a fault the OS sees only the current reference and the next 3.

steps.title: References 1–3: cold misses
steps.body: Pages 1, 3, 2 go into the three empty frames. Faults so far: **3**.

steps.title: Reference 4 (page 4): evict 1
steps.body: Frames hold 1, 3, 2. Window = refs 4–7 $= 4, 2, 3, 1$. Next uses: 2 at ref 5, 3 at ref 6, 1 at ref 7. Page 1 is used last, so evict **1**. Frames: 4, 3, 2. Faults: **4**.

steps.title: References 5–6: hits
steps.body: Pages 2 and 3 are both resident — two hits.

steps.title: Reference 7 (page 1): evict 3
steps.body: Frames hold 4, 3, 2. Window = refs 7–10 $= 1, 2, 4, 3$. Next uses: 2 at ref 8, 4 at ref 9, 3 at ref 10. Evict **3** (farthest). Frames: 4, 1, 2. Faults: **5**.

steps.title: References 8–9: hits
steps.body: Pages 2 and 4 are resident — two hits.

steps.title: Reference 10 (page 3): evict 2
steps.body: Frames hold 4, 1, 2. Only 3 references remain, so the window is refs 10–12 $= 3, 1, 4$. Page 2 does not appear in it, so evict **2**. Frames: 4, 1, 3. Faults: **6**.

steps.title: References 11–12: hits, total
steps.body:
Pages 1 and 4 are resident — two hits.

Total page faults $= 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6$.

cse-2025-1-cs-44.shortcut: Here the 4-reference window always contains enough information to make the same choice as full OPT, so a plain OPT simulation also gives 6 faults (3 cold + 3 replacements).
pitfalls: Using a window of 4 references *after* the current one: the question says the 4 include the current page.
At reference 10, hunting for the next use of page 2 beyond the window — with limited look-ahead, a page not in the window is the victim.
Counting the three cold misses as non-faults: loading into empty frames is still a page fault.
cse-2025-1-cs-44.verification: Count faults by type: 3 compulsory misses (1, 3, 2) + 3 replacement faults (at refs 4, 7, 10) $= 6$; the other 6 references are hits, and $6 + 6 = 12$ references.

cse-2025-1-cs-45.approach: Evaluate the uncorrelated subquery once: find Mark's cid, the team(s) he coaches, and the members of those teams. Then take the minimum age over those players.

steps.title: Mark's coach id
steps.body: `C.cname = 'Mark'` selects the coach row $(102, \text{Mark})$, so $C.cid = 102$.

steps.title: Teams coached by Mark
steps.body: `T.cid = C.cid = 102` keeps only team $(10, \text{MI}, \text{Mumbai}, 102)$, so $T.tid = 10$.

steps.title: Members of team 10
steps.body: `M.tid = T.tid = 10` keeps members $(1, 10)$ and $(3, 10)$. The subquery returns $\{1, 3\}$.

steps.title: Minimum age
steps.body:
Players with pid in $\{1, 3\}$: Jasprit (31) and Ishan (26).

$$\min(31, 26) = 26$$

cse-2025-1-cs-45.shortcut: Mark → cid 102 → team MI (tid 10) → players 1, 3 → ages 31, 26 → minimum 26.
pitfalls: Answering 24 — the minimum age of all players (Atharva, in team PK coached by Trevor).
Matching Mark to team DC because Mark's cid (102) appears in row 1 of coach and DC appears second in team — always join on cid, not on row position.
Thinking the comma join produces duplicates that change the answer: duplicates in an `IN` list do not matter, and MIN ignores multiplicity anyway.
cse-2025-1-cs-45.verification: Reverse check: player 3 (age 26) is in team 10 (members), team 10 has cid 102 (team), and 102 is Mark (coach). The only other qualifying player, 1, is older (31).

cse-2025-1-cs-46.approach: The message is error-free only if none of the 5 independent bits flips, so the probability is the product of the five per-bit success probabilities: $(1-0.01)^5$.

steps.title: One bit
steps.body: A bit arrives correctly with probability $1 - 0.01 = 0.99$.

steps.title: All five bits (independence)
steps.body:
$$P(\text{error-free}) = 0.99^5$$

This is the $k = 0$ term of $\text{Bin}(5, 0.01)$: $\binom{5}{0}(0.01)^0(0.99)^5$.

pitfalls: Stopping at the linear approximation $1 - 5(0.01) = 0.950$: the $+10(0.01)^2 = 0.001$ term changes the third decimal.
Computing $1 - 0.01^5$ (probability that not *all* bits flip) instead of the probability that *no* bit flips.
Answering $5 \times 0.01 \times 0.99^4 \approx 0.048$ — that is the probability of exactly one flipped bit.
cse-2025-1-cs-46.verification: Complement check: $P(\text{at least one flip}) = 1 - 0.95099 = 0.04901$, which is just under the union bound $5 \times 0.01 = 0.05$, as it must be.

cse-2025-1-cs-47.approach: Fragment hop by hop. Each fragment carries a 20-byte IPv4 header and (except the last) a payload that is a multiple of 8. Routers fragment but never reassemble, so fragments made at Router-1 are fragmented again independently at Router-2.
cse-2025-1-cs-47.given: Data = 15000 bytes, IPv4 header = 20 bytes (no options). MTU after Router-1 = 5000 bytes, after Router-2 = 3000 bytes (MTU includes the header).

steps.title: Payload limit at Router-1
steps.body: Max data per fragment $= 5000 - 20 = 4980$ bytes. Non-final fragments need data that is a multiple of 8: $\lfloor 4980/8 \rfloor \times 8 = 622 \times 8 = 4976$ bytes.

steps.title: Payload limit at Router-2
steps.body: Max data $= 3000 - 20 = 2980$; multiple of 8: $\lfloor 2980/8 \rfloor \times 8 = 372 \times 8 = 2976$ bytes.

steps.title: Router-2 re-fragments each piece
steps.body:
- Each 4976-byte fragment $\to 2976 + 2000$ (2 fragments; $4976 - 2976 = 2000$). Three of them give $3 \times 2 = 6$.
- The 72-byte fragment (92 bytes total) fits in 3000 → 1 fragment.

Total $= 6 + 1 = 7$ fragments reach the destination.

cse-2025-1-cs-47.shortcut: Fragments after Router-1: $\lceil 15000/4976 \rceil = 4$ (three full + 72). Each full 4976 needs $\lceil 4976/2976 \rceil = 2$ at Router-2, the small one 1: $3 \times 2 + 1 = 7$.
pitfalls: Fragmenting the original message directly for the smallest MTU: $\lceil 15000/2976 \rceil = 6$. Fragments created at Router-1 are not reassembled, so Router-2 works on them one by one.
Forgetting the 20-byte header (treating 5000 and 3000 as pure data): Router-1 makes 3 fragments of 5000, Router-2 splits each into 3000 + 2000, giving 6 — wrong.
Ignoring the multiple-of-8 rule. (Here 4980/2980 would still give 7, but in general offsets are in 8-byte units and the data sizes must be 4976 and 2976.)
cse-2025-1-cs-47.verification: Data is conserved: $3 \times (2976 + 2000) + 72 = 3 \times 4976 + 72 = 15000$ bytes, and every delivered fragment is at most $2976 + 20 = 2996 \le 3000$ bytes.

cse-2025-1-cs-48.approach: Use the normalisation condition $\int P(x)\,dx = 1$ to find $C$, then integrate the density from 2 to 3. Both integrals are of $x^2$, so everything reduces to differences of cubes.

steps.title: Find C
steps.body: $$\int_1^4 Cx^2\,dx = C\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4 = C\cdot\frac{64 - 1}{3} = 21C = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; C = \frac{1}{21}$$

cse-2025-1-cs-48.shortcut: For a density $\propto x^2$ on $[a, b]$: $P(c \le x \le d) = \dfrac{d^3 - c^3}{b^3 - a^3} = \dfrac{27 - 8}{64 - 1} = \dfrac{19}{63}$.
pitfalls: Normalising over $[0, 4]$ instead of $[1, 4]$: $C = 3/64$ and the answer becomes $19/64 \approx 0.297$.
Forgetting the $1/3$ from integrating $x^2$ in only one of the two integrals.
Truncating $0.30159$ to $0.301$ instead of rounding to $0.302$.

cse-2025-1-cs-49.approach: Partition refinement (Moore's algorithm) for a Mealy machine: first group states by their output pair $(f_{X=0}, f_{X=1})$, then repeatedly split a group whenever its members go, on some input, to different groups. Stop when nothing splits; the number of groups is the minimum number of states.

steps.title: Split {A, B, C, E}
steps.body:
Look at the $X = 0$ successors: A $\to$ F, C $\to$ F (group $\{F\}$) but B $\to$ D, E $\to$ D (group $\{D,H\}$). So the block splits into $\{A, C\}$ and $\{B, E\}$.

The $X = 1$ successors (B, C, E, C) all lie in $\{A,B,C,E\}$, so they cause no further split here.

steps.title: {D, H} stays together
steps.body:
D and H have identical rows: next states (G, A), outputs (1, 0). They are equivalent.

$$P_1 = \{A,C\},\ \{B,E\},\ \{D,H\},\ \{F\},\ \{G\}$$

steps.title: Check P1 is stable
steps.body:
- $\{A,C\}$: $X=0$: F, F (same); $X=1$: B, E — both in $\{B,E\}$. Stable.
- $\{B,E\}$: identical rows (D, C). Stable.
- $\{D,H\}$: identical rows. Stable.

No block splits, so $P_2 = P_1$ and the minimum number of states is **5**: $\{A,C\}, \{B,E\}, \{D,H\}, F, G$.

cse-2025-1-cs-49.shortcut: Spot identical rows first: B ≡ E (same next states and outputs) and D ≡ H. Replacing E by B and H by D makes rows A and C identical (F, B / 0, 0), so A ≡ C. $8 - 3 = 5$ states.
pitfalls: Merging A, B, C, E because they have the same outputs — equal outputs are only the starting partition; B and E go to D on $X = 0$ while A and C go to F.
Treating the outputs as Moore outputs (one per state) — here the output depends on the input too, so compare the whole pair $(f_0, f_1)$.
Missing A ≡ C because their $X = 1$ successors (B and E) are different letters — they are in the same block, which is all that matters.
cse-2025-1-cs-49.verification: The reduced machine is consistent: with classes $a = \{A,C\}$, $b = \{B,E\}$, $d = \{D,H\}$: $a: (F, b)$, $b: (d, a)$, $d: (G, a)$, $F: (F, b)$, $G: (G, d)$ — every original row maps to exactly one reduced row, and F, G, $d$, $a$/$b$ have pairwise different output pairs or successors.

cse-2025-1-cs-50.approach: Read the wiring: $D_1 = Q_0$, $D_2 = Q_1$, $D_3 = Q_2$ and $D_0 = \overline{Q_3}$. That is a 4-bit twisted-ring (Johnson) counter, which cycles through $2n = 8$ states. Tracing from any start state confirms the cycle length.

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body:
On each clock edge every D flip-flop copies its D input:

$$Q_0^+ = \overline{Q_3},\quad Q_1^+ = Q_0,\quad Q_2^+ = Q_1,\quad Q_3^+ = Q_2$$

The register shifts right and feeds the complement of the last bit back in.

steps.title: Trace from 0000
steps.body:
Writing states as $Q_0Q_1Q_2Q_3$: $0000 \to 1000 \to 1100 \to 1110 \to 1111 \to 0111 \to 0011 \to 0001 \to 0000$.

The ones fill in from the left, then the zeros do.

steps.title: Count the states
steps.body: The cycle contains **8** distinct states ($2n$ for $n = 4$). Starting from the initial state, the circuit goes through 8 distinct states (the initial one included) before it is back where it started — 7 others besides the initial state, which is why the official key accepts 7 to 8.

steps.title: Any initial value gives 8
steps.body: The 8 states not in the main cycle form a second cycle of the same length: $0100 \to 1010 \to 1101 \to 0110 \to 1011 \to 0101 \to 0010 \to 1001 \to 0100$. So the answer does not depend on the (unspecified) initial value.

answer.value: The counter cycles through **8** distinct states (key accepts 7 to 8)

cse-2025-1-cs-50.shortcut: Shift register with inverted feedback from the last stage to the first = Johnson counter: $2n = 2 \times 4 = 8$ states.
pitfalls: Taking the feedback from $Q_3$ instead of $\overline{Q_3}$: that is a ring counter, whose cycle length depends on the initial value (e.g. 4 for 1000, 1 for 0000).
Answering $2^4 = 16$ — a Johnson counter uses only $2n$ of the $2^n$ states.
Assuming an unused (lock-out) start state gives a different count: here the other 8 states also form an 8-cycle.
cse-2025-1-cs-50.verification: Both cycles together cover $8 + 8 = 16 = 2^4$ states, each exactly once, so every start value returns after exactly 8 clocks.

animation.title: States Q0 Q1 Q2 Q3 (D0 = Q3′)

cse-2025-1-cs-51.approach: `foo` walks the array once: it adds 1 for every adjacent pair that differs and returns 1 at the last element. So it counts the number of **runs** (maximal blocks of equal values) — boundaries + 1.

steps.title: What foo computes
steps.body:
`foo(S, n)` compares `S[0]` with `S[1]`, then recurses on the suffix `S+1` of length $n-1$. Unrolled:

$$\text{foo}(A, 9) = \#\{i : A[i] \ne A[i+1],\ 0 \le i \le 7\} + 1$$

The final `+1` comes from the base case `size == 1`.

steps.title: Add the base case
steps.body:
$$\text{foo}(A, 9) = 4 + 1 = 5$$

Indeed the runs are $[0], [1], [2,2,2], [0,0], [1,1]$ — five of them. The program prints **5**.

pitfalls: Counting distinct values (3: 0, 1, 2) — values that reappear later start a new run.
Forgetting the `return 1` at `size == 1`, giving 4 (just the number of changes).
Thinking `size == 0` is ever reached from `foo(A, 9)` — recursion stops at size 1.
cse-2025-1-cs-51.verification: Full unrolling: $1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0$ from the 8 comparisons, plus 1 from the base case, $= 5$.

cse-2025-1-cs-52.approach: Trace the loop. `ptr1` always looks at its **next** node: if that node's value occurs in L2 it is unlinked (and `ptr1` stays put), otherwise `ptr1` advances. So every node except the head whose value is in L2 is removed; the head is never examined.

steps.title: Start: ptr1 at the head (1)
steps.body: The head 1 is never tested — the loop only checks `ptr1->next`. Next is 7: not in L2, so `ptr1` moves to 7.

steps.title: Next = 12: in L2, delete
steps.body: `find(12, L2)` = 1, so `7->next = 3`. Node 12 is unlinked; `ptr1` stays at 7.

steps.title: Next = 3: keep; next = 9: delete
steps.body: 3 is not in L2 → `ptr1` moves to 3. Then 9 is in L2 → `3->next = 5`, 9 removed.

steps.title: Next = 5: keep; 11 and 15: delete
steps.body: 5 not in L2 → `ptr1` moves to 5. Then 11 in L2 → removed; the new next is 15, also in L2 → removed. Now `5->next = 8`.

steps.title: Next = 8: keep; loop ends
steps.body:
8 is not in L2 → `ptr1` moves to 8, whose `next` is NULL, so the loop stops.

L1 is now $1 \to 7 \to 3 \to 5 \to 8$: **5** nodes.

cse-2025-1-cs-52.shortcut: Values of L1 after the head that are in L2: 12, 9, 11, 15 (four). $9 - 4 = 5$ nodes; the head 1 survives even though 1 is in L2.
pitfalls: Deleting the head 1 too (it is in L2) and answering 4 — the code only ever tests `ptr1->next`.
Advancing `ptr1` after a deletion: then two consecutive matches (11, 15) would let 15 survive, giving 6.
Counting 12 as missing from L2 — L2 contains 12 (sixth node).
cse-2025-1-cs-52.verification: Set check: L1 values after the head are $\{7, 12, 3, 9, 5, 11, 15, 8\}$; minus L2 gives $\{7, 3, 5, 8\}$ (4 nodes), plus the head = 5 nodes.

cse-2025-1-cs-53.approach: `t` becomes the place value of the leading digit, then the loop peels digits off from the left. `turn` alternates 0, 1, 0, 1, …, and a digit is appended to `newnum` only when `turn` is 1 — i.e. the 2nd, 4th, … digits from the left.

steps.title: Digits 1 and 4
steps.body:
Iteration 1: $d = 14362/10000 = 1$, $n = 4362$, $t = 1000$; turn = 0 → skip; turn becomes 1.

Iteration 2: $d = 4362/1000 = 4$, $n = 362$, $t = 100$; turn = 1 → newnum $= 10 \times 0 + 4 = 4$; turn becomes 0.

steps.title: Digits 3 and 6
steps.body:
Iteration 3: $d = 362/100 = 3$, $n = 62$, $t = 10$; turn = 0 → skip; turn becomes 1.

Iteration 4: $d = 62/10 = 6$, $n = 2$, $t = 1$; turn = 1 → newnum $= 10 \times 4 + 6 = 46$; turn becomes 0.

steps.title: Digit 2 and return
steps.body:
Iteration 5: $d = 2/1 = 2$, $n = 0$, $t = 0$; turn = 0 → skip. Now $t = 0$, the loop ends and `gate` returns 46.

The program prints **46**.

cse-2025-1-cs-53.shortcut: Keep the even-position digits from the left of 1 4 3 6 2: positions 2 and 4 are 4 and 6 → 46.
pitfalls: Taking the odd positions (1, 3, 2 → 132) — `turn` starts at 0, so the first digit is skipped.
Stopping `t` at 10000 too early or late: the loop exits with $t = 100000$, then divides once to 10000.
Reading digits from the right (the code divides by a decreasing power of 10, so it reads left to right).
cse-2025-1-cs-53.verification: Pattern check with another input: for `gate(123456)` the same logic keeps digits 2, 4, 6 → 246, consistent with "even positions from the left"; for 14362 that gives 46.

cse-2025-1-cs-54.approach: An edge $(B, C)$ is in **every** MST exactly when it is strictly lighter than the heaviest edge on every other B–C path (cycle property). So $x$ must be smaller than the minimax ("bottleneck") B–C path weight in the graph without edge BC.
cse-2025-1-cs-54.given: Edges: AB = 7, AD = 6, DC = 8, BD = 1, AC = 3, BC = $x$.

steps.title: Condition for BC to be in every MST
steps.body:
Cycle property: BC can be left out of *some* MST iff there is a B–C path (avoiding BC) whose every edge has weight $\le x$. So BC is in every MST iff

$$x < \min_{\text{B–C paths}} \big(\max \text{ edge on the path}\big).$$

steps.title: Bottleneck of each B–C path
steps.body:
| path | edges | max |
|---|---|---|
| B–D–A–C | 1, 6, 3 | 6 |
| B–A–C | 7, 3 | 7 |
| B–D–C | 1, 8 | 8 |
| B–A–D–C | 7, 6, 8 | 8 |

The best (smallest) bottleneck is **6**, via B–D–A–C.

steps.title: Largest integer x
steps.body:
BC is in every MST iff $x < 6$, so the maximum integer value is $x = 5$.

Check $x = 5$ with Kruskal: BD (1), AC (3), then BC (5) joins $\{B, D\}$ and $\{A, C\}$ → MST $= \{1, 3, 5\}$, weight 9, unique.

steps.title: Why not x = 6
steps.body: With $x = 6$, BC ties with AD. Kruskal may take AD (6) instead of BC, giving the MST $\{BD, AC, AD\}$ of weight $1 + 3 + 6 = 10$ that does **not** contain BC. So $x = 6$ fails the "every MST" requirement.

scene.caption: x = 6: an MST without BC exists

cse-2025-1-cs-54.shortcut: Run Kruskal without BC: BD (1), AC (3), AD (6) connects everything. BC must beat the edge that finally joins B's side to C's side, AD = 6, strictly: $x \le 5$.
pitfalls: Answering 6: with a tie, BC is in *some* MST but not in *every* MST.
Comparing $x$ only with the edges incident to B or C (e.g. $x < 7$ because of AB) instead of with the bottleneck path B–D–A–C.
Swapping the diagonal weights (BD = 3, AC = 1) does not change the answer: the bottleneck of B–D–A–C is still AD = 6.
cse-2025-1-cs-54.verification: For $x = 5$ every other B–C path has a maximum edge $\ge 6 > 5$, so BC is never the heaviest edge of any cycle; for $x = 6$ the cycle B–C–A–D–B has two maximum edges (BC and AD), so BC can be dropped.

cse-2025-1-cs-55.approach: Insert the keys in order. For each key compute $h_1(k) = k \bmod 11$; on a collision step by $h_2(k) = 1 + (k \bmod 7)$, probing $(h_1 + i\,h_2) \bmod 11$ for $i = 0, 1, 2, \dots$. Only the final key 24 collides.

steps.title: Insert 79, 67
steps.body:
- $79 \bmod 11 = 2$ ($79 = 7\times11 + 2$) → slot 2.
- $67 \bmod 11 = 1$ ($67 = 6\times11 + 1$) → slot 1.

No collisions.

steps.title: Key 24 stored in slot 10
steps.body: Key 24 goes into slot **10**.

pitfalls: Using $h_2(k) = k \bmod 7$ without the $+1$: step 3 gives probes 2, 5 → slot 5.
Linear probing out of habit: 2, 3, 4 → slot 4.
Arithmetic slips in $k \bmod 11$ (e.g. $79 \bmod 11 = 2$, not 3) that create or hide collisions.
cse-2025-1-cs-55.verification: Final table: slot 1 = 67, 2 = 79, 3 = 25, 6 = 50, 8 = 63, 10 = 24 — six distinct slots for six keys, and 24's probes 2 and 6 are exactly the slots taken before it. (The official key accepts 10 to 11, which presumably also covers 1-based slot numbering; with 0-based slots as in $k \bmod 11$ the answer is 10.)
